analysis.title: SMCI, NVDA: Do we need to add a smuggling line to our SMCI revenue build?
key_insights: On Thursday 3/19 after the close, federal prosecutors unsealed an indictment in New York charging three SMCI-linked individuals (two employees, one contractor) with conspiring to illegally divert Nvidia GPUs to China in violation of US export controls. Two were arrested, including SMCI co-founder and board director Wally Liaw.

The indictment alleges $2.5bn worth of AI servers were illegally diverted to China. SMCI is not named as a defendant, has put the two employees on administrative leave and has terminated the contractor relationship. SMCI shares were down 23% at time of writing.

The case is separate from the February 2025 Singapore fraud case, in which three individuals were charged with defrauding SMCI and Dell by misrepresenting the end destinations and end users of AI servers containing Nvidia GPUs. Bernstein says the goal appears the same: diverting Nvidia GPUs to China.

Liaw resigned in 2018 after the first accounting scandal, was rehired and reappointed to the board in 2023, and was named in a 2024 lawsuit alleging improper revenue recognition. Bernstein says the key question is whether this is an isolated 'rogue employees' case or evidence of systemic compliance gaps in SMCI's global sales and channel operations.

Bernstein says the credibility issues could affect SMCI's business even though SMCI is not a defendant. If Nvidia distances itself from SMCI, SMCI's GPU supply could be hurt, which Bernstein says could have a devastating impact on SMCI.

Bernstein sees no fault on Nvidia's part. The indictment does not suggest Nvidia had any knowledge of the scheme, and Bernstein is confident Nvidia takes export control responsibilities extremely seriously.

SMCI is rated Market-Perform with a $37 PT, set at 14x FY27 EPS of $2.67 (in line with the 5-year average PE of 13.95x). Bernstein calls SMCI an early leader and current #2 AI server OEM, but the accounting history and the resurfaced China-smuggling concerns give it pause.
NVDA is rated Outperform with a $300 PT, set at about 25x FY28 (CY27) non-GAAP EPS of $11.94. Bernstein says the datacenter opportunity is enormous, still early, with material upside possible.
Bernstein lists any new accounting issues or concerns about circumventing US-China trade restrictions as the biggest downside risk to SMCI, as they could cause a crisis in confidence.

market_movers.rationale: Bernstein keeps Market-Perform and a $37 PT (14x FY27 EPS of $2.67) after the indictment. Accounting history and the resurfaced China GPU-diversion concerns give it pause. The closing price of $30.79 on 3/19 implies 37.7% above current price per the ticker table's 'Rel. Perf.' column, and the stock was down 23% after the news.
Bernstein sees no fault on Nvidia's part in the indictment and calls the datacenter opportunity enormous and still early. PT is about 25x FY28 (CY27) non-GAAP EPS of $11.94.

sector_views.rationale: SMCI is described as an early leader and current #2 AI server OEM. Compliance and accounting concerns are the swing factor for SMCI specifically, while Nvidia is viewed as unaffected.

earnings_insights: SMCI Bernstein estimates: adjusted EPS $2.04 (2025A), $2.27 (2026E), $2.67 (2027E). Adjusted P/E 15.1x, 13.6x and 11.5x respectively on the 3/19 close of $30.79.
NVDA Bernstein estimates (base year FY2026): adjusted EPS $4.77 (2025A), $8.88 (2026E), $11.94 (2027E). Adjusted P/E 37.4x, 20.1x and 15.0x respectively on the 3/19 close of $178.56.
risk_factors: Nvidia could further distance itself from SMCI, which could cut SMCI's GPU supply.
Evidence of systemic compliance gaps in SMCI's global sales and channel operations rather than isolated rogue employees.
New accounting issues or concerns around circumventing US-China trade restrictions could cause a crisis in confidence in SMCI.

NVDA downside risks: lumpiness in near-term business trends, slower revenue growth in key end markets, competitor pressure on share or pricing, customers migrating to internal silicon, and regulatory risks around technology exports.
geopolitical: US-China technology export controls: federal indictment alleges diversion of Nvidia GPUs in AI servers to China in violation of US export rules, with $2.5bn of servers alleged to have been diverted.

Earlier Singapore case filed in February 2025 against three individuals (two Singaporeans and one Chinese national) for defrauding SMCI and Dell over the final destinations and end users of AI servers with Nvidia GPUs.

tension_points.bull_case: The indictment may be an isolated case of rogue employees. SMCI is not named as a defendant, has put the two employees on administrative leave and terminated the contractor relationship. Bernstein sees no Nvidia fault, so the GPU supply relationship may be unaffected.
tension_points.bear_case: The case may be evidence of systemic compliance gaps in SMCI's global sales and channel operations. The accused includes a co-founder rehired to the board in 2023 after the 2018 accounting scandal, and a second diversion case, Singapore in February 2025, also involved SMCI servers. Nvidia could distance itself and curtail GPU supply, which Bernstein says could have a devastating impact on SMCI.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Nvidia curtailing or distancing itself from SMCI on GPU supply would invalidate the isolated-incident read.

theme_stances.key_argument: The indictment raises serious credibility issues for SMCI that could affect its business and its Nvidia GPU supply, even though SMCI is not a defendant.
theme_stances.evidence: this raises serious credibility issues that could impact business
